title: Fast/slow pointers (tortoise & hare)
description: Two pointers from head — slow advances by 1, fast by 2. The boilerplate behind cycle detection, midpoint, and Nth-from-end.

conversation.intro: This is a syntax-template lesson — the fast/slow (tortoise-and-hare) two-pointer skeleton. The interview script focuses on the three classic uses and the loop-guard discipline. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. When do you reach for fast/slow?
sections.prompt: Three problem signatures that all reduce to the same loop.
sections.say:
"Fast/slow is one boilerplate with three classic uses:

• CYCLE DETECTION — `if (slow === fast) return true` inside the loop, `return false` on fall-through. If a cycle exists, fast laps slow inside it because the gap closes by 1 per iteration. If no cycle, fast hits null first.

• MIDDLE NODE — when the loop exits cleanly (no cycle), slow is at the midpoint. For odd length n, slow is at the true center (index (n-1)/2). For even length n, slow lands on the SECOND of the two middles (index n/2).

• NTH FROM END — advance fast by N first, THEN move both together until fast is null. Slow ends N nodes from the end.

The loop body — `slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next;` — is identical across all three. Only the guard and the per-iteration check differ."
sections.why: Naming the boilerplate as a boilerplate AND listing the three uses is the fluency move. Most candidates treat 'Linked List Cycle', 'Middle of the Linked List', and 'Remove Nth From End' as three separate problems; the candidate who's drilled this family writes the same scaffold for all three. Interviewers grade on that recognition. The 'slow lands on the SECOND middle for even length' callout is the exact bit of knowledge interviewers check — most candidates guess wrong and have to trace it out.

sections.title: 2. Why fast/slow, not a hash set or a length pass?
sections.prompt: Defend the two-pointer trick against the obvious alternatives.
sections.say:
"For cycle detection, the naive solution is a hash Set: walk the list, store each node, return true the moment you see one twice. That's O(n) time but O(n) extra space. Fast/slow gets the same correctness in O(1) space — two pointer variables, no auxiliary structure. The math: if there's a cycle, fast moves 2 and slow moves 1, so the gap shrinks by 1 each iteration once both are inside the cycle. After at most C iterations (cycle length) they collide. If no cycle, fast hits null in at most n/2 iterations.

For middle node, the naive solution is two passes: walk once to count nodes, then walk again to index n/2. That's still O(n) time but two passes. Fast/slow does it in ONE pass: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. Same time bound, half the actual work.

The shared idea — and what makes this a TEMPLATE rather than three separate tricks — is that running two pointers at different speeds extracts structural information about the list (cycle? half-length? Nth-from-end?) in a single walk."
sections.why: Naming the alternative algorithms (hash set, two-pass) and explaining what fast/slow buys over them is the move that proves you didn't just memorize the trick. Interviewers worry about candidates who deploy the clever solution without acknowledging the simpler one — the better signal is 'I know three solutions, here's why I picked this one'. The 'extracts structural information in one walk' framing is what unifies the three uses.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern: which variant?
sections.prompt: How to decide given a new linked-list problem.
sections.say:
"The decision rule:

1. Does the problem mention CYCLES or 'is this list circular'? → Floyd cycle detection. Loop with `slow === fast` check inside.
2. Does the problem ask for the MIDDLE or 'middle element' or split the list in half? → Midpoint variant. Loop with no inner check, return `slow` after.
3. Does the problem ask for the Nth FROM END, or 'remove Nth from end'? → Head-start variant. Advance fast by N first, then advance both together until fast is null.
4. Does the problem involve splitting/reorganizing in linear space (like reorder list, palindrome list)? → Midpoint variant is usually phase 1.
5. If 'O(1) extra space' is in the constraints AND it's a list problem → fast/slow is almost certainly the answer.

The loop guard is the same in all variants: `while (fast && fast.next)`. The differences are in what you do INSIDE the loop and what you RETURN."
sections.why: Walking through the decision tree shows the FAMILY, not just the templates. Most candidates pick the variant by gut feel; running the explicit check ('does the problem mention cycles?') makes the choice principled. The 'O(1) extra space + linked list = fast/slow' shortcut is the killer heuristic — once you see those two signals together, the answer is forced.

sections.title: 4. Trace through a tiny example
sections.prompt: Walk the midpoint case on two lengths so the 'slow lands on second middle' rule lands.
sections.intro: "Let me trace `middleValue` on an odd-length list and an even-length list to confirm where slow lands in each case."

examples.note: Odd length — slow lands on the true middle (index 2 of 5).
examples.trace:
init: slow=1, fast=1
iter1: slow=2, fast=3. fast && fast.next → continue.
iter2: slow=3, fast=5. fast && fast.next? fast.next=null → exit loop.
return slow.val = 3 ✓

examples.note: Even length — there's no single true middle; slow lands on the second of the two (index n/2 = 2). Predict this in interviews, don't guess.
examples.trace:
init: slow=1, fast=1
iter1: slow=2, fast=3. fast && fast.next → continue.
iter2: slow=3, fast=null. fast && fast.next? fast=null → exit loop.
return slow.val = 3 ✓ (the second middle, NOT 2)

examples.note: Single node — loop guard `fast && fast.next` is immediately false (fast.next is null), so slow stays at head.
examples.trace:
init: slow=1, fast=1
loop guard: fast=1, fast.next=null → exit immediately.
return slow.val = 1 ✓

sections.why: Running BOTH parities side-by-side is the move — the 'slow lands on second middle for even length' rule is the question interviewers love to ask, and seeing it concretely on `[1,2,3,4]` is much more memorable than memorizing the rule. The single-node trace defends the loop guard: `fast && fast.next` correctly bails when fast.next is null, no special case needed.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Pitfalls when you drop fast/slow into a real problem:
• Empty list (head=null) → loop guard `fast && fast.next` is false immediately. `slow` stays null; returning `slow.val` would throw, so handle empty separately if the problem allows it.
• Single node → loop guard is false (fast.next is null); slow stays at head. For cycle detection: return false. For midpoint: return head. Both correct.
• Two nodes (even length=2) → loop runs once: slow=node2, fast=null. slow lands on the SECOND middle (node 2). Sanity-check this — easy to expect node 1.
• Loop guard MUST be `fast && fast.next` — if you wrote just `while (fast)`, then `fast.next.next` would throw the moment `fast.next` is null. Both checks are non-negotiable because fast does a double-hop.
• Use `===` for the cycle meeting check, not `slow.val === fast.val`. Two distinct nodes can hold the same value, which would give false positives.
• Cycle in the input when you didn't expect one → midpoint variant would loop forever. If cycles are possible, run cycle detection first OR cap iterations as defensive code.
• Off-by-one in the Nth-from-end variant — advance fast by EXACTLY N (not N-1 or N+1), then advance both together. The N-step head start is exactly the gap you want preserved.
• Forgetting that for even length, slow lands on the SECOND middle — interviews love this trick question."
sections.why: The loop-guard bug — `while (fast)` instead of `while (fast && fast.next)` — is the canonical fast/slow foot-gun and the first thing an interviewer will probe. Calling it out unprompted is fluency. The 'second middle for even length' rule is the other classic gotcha; naming it before the interviewer asks earns the senior signal. The value-equality vs reference-equality bug is subtle but real — two distinct nodes can share a value, and `=== ` is the only safe comparison.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & common follow-ups
sections.prompt: What does the template cost, and what problems use it?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — slow visits at most n nodes; fast visits at most 2n; both bounded by n. For cycle detection specifically, the amortized bound is 2n iterations (once both pointers are in the cycle, the gap closes by 1 per iteration, so they meet within C iterations where C ≤ n).

Space is O(1) — two pointer variables, no auxiliary data structure. This is the whole point — it's why fast/slow beats the hash-set version of cycle detection.

Common follow-ups that USE this template as the skeleton:
• Linked List Cycle (LeetCode 141) → the canonical cycle-detection variant.
• Linked List Cycle II (LeetCode 142) → find WHERE the cycle starts, using a clever second pass after the meeting point.
• Middle of the Linked List (LeetCode 876) → the canonical midpoint variant.
• Remove Nth From End (LeetCode 19) → head-start variant.
• Reorder List (LeetCode 143) → midpoint + reverse + merge (composes multiple templates).
• Palindrome Linked List (LeetCode 234) → midpoint + reverse second half + compare.
• Happy Number (LeetCode 202) → fast/slow on an IMPLICIT graph (numbers, not nodes) — same template, different domain.
• Find the Duplicate Number (LeetCode 287) → fast/slow on an implicit functional graph defined by `nums[i]` — same template again.

The last two are the senior-tier extensions — they show fast/slow isn't a linked-list trick, it's a CYCLE-IN-FUNCTIONAL-GRAPH trick that happens to apply to linked lists naturally."
sections.why: Listing the family — including the two implicit-graph extensions (Happy Number, Find the Duplicate) — is what proves you see fast/slow as a CYCLE-IN-A-FUNCTIONAL-GRAPH technique, not just a linked-list trick. Interviewers love this transfer because it means you'll pattern-match fast/slow onto problems that don't even use linked lists. That's the difference between drilled boilerplate and conceptual fluency.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical fast/slow midpoint finder — `middleValue(head)` — on three list lengths. Watch slow advance by 1 and fast by 2 per iteration, with the loop guard `fast && fast.next` catching the end. For even length, slow lands on the SECOND middle.
trace: const toArr = (n) => { const out = []; while (n) { out.push(n.val); n = n.next; } return out; };
const dummy = { val: null, next: null };
for (const v of input) { tail.next = { val: v, next: null }; tail = tail.next; }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter middleValue — list ${JSON.stringify(input)} (length ${input.length})`, state: { input, list: toArr(head) } };

yield { line: 2, label: `init slow=${slow ? slow.val : 'null'}, fast=${fast ? fast.val : 'null'} (both at head)`, state: { list: toArr(head), slow: slow ? slow.val : null, fast: fast ? fast.val : null } };

yield { line: 3, label: `loop guard ok (iter ${iter}) — fast=${fast.val}, fast.next=${fast.next.val} (both non-null, safe to double-hop)`, state: { iter, list: toArr(head), slow: slow.val, fast: fast.val } };
yield { line: 4, label: `slow += 1 → ${slow ? slow.val : 'null'}`, state: { iter, list: toArr(head), slow: slow ? slow.val : null, fast: fast.val } };
yield { line: 5, label: `fast += 2 → ${fast ? fast.val : 'null'}`, state: { iter, list: toArr(head), slow: slow ? slow.val : null, fast: fast ? fast.val : null } };

yield { line: 7, label: `loop exit — fast=${fast ? fast.val : 'null'}${fast ? `, fast.next=null` : ''} → slow is at the midpoint`, state: { iter, list: toArr(head), slow: slow ? slow.val : null, fast: fast ? fast.val : null } };
yield { line: 7, label: `return slow.val = ${ans}`, state: { list: toArr(head), midpoint: ans, returns: ans } };

notes: The loop condition `fast && fast.next` is non-negotiable: fast.next must be non-null before you can dereference fast.next.next, or you'll throw.
If slow === fast inside the loop, a cycle exists (fast lapped slow). If the loop exits cleanly, no cycle.
For even-length lists, slow lands on the SECOND of the two middle nodes — predict this in interviews instead of guessing.
Compare nodes with === (reference equality), never by .val — two distinct nodes can share a value.

questions.q: Why must the loop condition be `while (fast && fast.next)`?
options: Equivalent to `while (fast)` — JS short-circuits both `fast.next` and `fast.next.next` to undefined on a missing chain
fast moves two .next hops; both must be legal or `fast.next.next` throws
To ensure slow and fast meet on the same node when the cycle length is even (without it, they pass through each other)
Without it, even-length lists return the first middle instead of the second
questions.explain: Without the fast.next guard, dereferencing fast.next.next when fast.next is null throws a TypeError.

questions.q: If `slow === fast` becomes true inside the loop, what does that prove?
options: The two pointers are on nodes that hold the same value (which may or may not indicate a cycle)
A cycle exists — fast lapped slow
Slow has reached the cycle's entry node (the start of the loop, not the meeting point)
The remaining nodes form a palindrome around the current position
questions.explain: In a cyclic list the fast pointer eventually catches the slow pointer from behind. In an acyclic list fast hits null first.

questions.q: For an even-length list (e.g., 1→2→3→4), where does slow end up when the loop exits cleanly (no cycle)?
options: On the first of the two middle nodes (node 2)
On the second of the two middle nodes (node 3)
Halfway between nodes 2 and 3 — there's no integer midpoint, so slow.next is null and slow.val is undefined
On the last node (node 4) — fast hits null one iteration after slow finishes the list
questions.explain: After two iterations: slow goes head→2→3, fast goes head→3→null. slow ends at the second middle (node 3).

questions.q: To find the Nth node from the end with fast/slow pointers, you:
options: Advance both together until fast hits null
Advance fast by N first, then advance both together until fast is null
Advance slow by N first, then move fast alone
Walk the list twice — once to count, once to index
questions.explain: The N-step head start on fast is exactly the gap you want to preserve as both walk together.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the tortoise-and-hare loop that detects a cycle. (The list a→b→c→a is built for you.)
Fill in the midpoint finder. When the loop exits, slow is at the middle node.

L3.prompt: Write `middleValue(head)` that returns the value at the midpoint using fast/slow pointers. For the even-length list 1→2→3→4, slow lands on the SECOND middle (value 3). Log the result.
hints: slow advances by 1, fast by 2. Loop while fast AND fast.next are truthy.
When fast reaches the end, slow is at the midpoint. For even length, slow lands on the second of the two middles.
